variants.name: Discriminated union + transition functions
variants.idiom_name: discriminated-union state + transition functions typed by their legal source state
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript's structural type system makes the union form the compact replacement for the classic structure: model each state as a tagged object type, write each transition as a function that accepts only its legal source states and returns the next state type, and the compiler rejects ship(pending) without any runtime guard. For fluent APIs the second realization threads a state type parameter (class SafeUserBuilder<S extends State>) through the chain and narrows the terminal method's this type, which is how staged builders enforce required fields. Either way the check is erased at run time - JavaScript can call around it - so keep runtime validation at trust boundaries.
pitfalls: A union value still carries its tag at run time and can be cast (as Paid) or widened to any; the guarantee holds only for code that neither casts nor escapes.
Widening a state to the full union inside a helper re-introduces runtime narrowing and loses the per-transition check that made the pattern worthwhile.
Structural typing lets an object with the same fields satisfy a state type; brand the states (a unique symbol or a private brand) when accidental compatibility would be unsound.

variants.name: State type parameter threaded through a fluent builder
variants.idiom_name: state type parameter on the builder + this-narrowed terminal method
variants.implementation_notes: The builder carries the accumulated state as a type parameter and each setter returns a new instantiation with one more flag set (S & { name: true }), while build() narrows its this type so it is callable only when the required flags are present. Choose it for chained APIs - query builders and staged form builders - where the state is a set of satisfied requirements rather than a lifecycle.
pitfalls: Each setter needs a generic return type; returning `this` naively widens the state and disables the check.
Accumulated intersections produce unsatisfiable types after a typo in a flag name, and the error surfaces at build() rather than at the offending setter.
